title: Reconcile token credits across protocol transforms (HTTP ↔ WS transcoding)
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We have observed divergences in per-request token accounting when the frontend protocol is HTTP (request/response) but the backend serving layer switches to WebSocket streaming for long responses. Root causes appear to be: (1) tokenization differences between client-side pre-tokenization and server-side tokenizer (leading to off-by-N credits), (2) framing boundaries and retransmits causing duplicate or orphaned fragments to be credited, (3) protocol transcoding that introduces an extra layer of chunking where prefix tokens are re-counted on resume or replay, and (4) inconsistent attribution of input tokens vs generated tokens when a request is proxied through the transcoder.

Impact: Customers using HTTP-to-WS transcoding (e.g., mobile clients using long-poll fallbacks, proxies that convert to streaming for cost/latency optimizations) report overcharges or missing token credits in edge conditions: connection drops with resume, client retries, and proxy-level buffering. This makes SLAs and invoices unreliable and causes support escalations.

Goal: Produce a deterministic, auditable reconciliation algorithm and implementation that ensures token credits are: (a) stable under protocol transition (HTTP <-> WS), (b) idempotent on retries and reconnections, and (c) attributable to the originating request or session in a single canonical place in the pipeline.

Scope: Investigate both runtime path and billing pipeline changes required: request fingerprinting through transcoding, canonical tokenization point, idempotency keys for frames/chunks, canonical finalization hooks for partially streamed responses, and audit logs for post-hoc reconciliation.

Non-Goals: Changes to customer-facing pricing models. We will not alter tokenization models for customers; instead we standardize where and how token counts are measured.

Acceptance criteria:
- A design doc describing the canonical measurement point (server-side tokenizer in the serving runtime) and how the transcoder emits token metadata to preserve attribution.
- A prototype schema for frame metadata (idempotency-key, sequence-offset, canonical-token-count, checksum) and an RFC for the transcoding protocol.
- Unit + integration tests showing deterministic token counts for the following scenarios: simple HTTP request->WS stream success; HTTP request with immediate client retry (idempotency); mid-stream disconnect + resume; proxy-induced buffering + replay; multipart attachments where content-length differs from tokenized length.
- End-to-end dashboard metrics and a reconciliation job demonstrating zero unexplained variance (<= 0.1%) across a 24h production-like replay workload.
- A migration plan and runtime feature flag to enable rollout with a canary group.

Proposed approach / Implementation notes:
1) Canonical tokenizer: instrument the serving runtime to emit canonical token counts at the first point of truth (post-model-tokenization step). Any upstream component (transcoder/proxy) must attach an idempotency header and preserve server-assigned frame IDs.
2) Frame metadata: standardize a compact JSON header per frame: {idempotency_key, frame_seq, canonical_token_count, checksum, final_frame_boolean}. Storing this metadata in the streaming coordinator lets the metering pipeline attribute tokens once final_frame_boolean is observed.
3) Deduplication window: implement a short-lived dedupe table keyed by (idempotency_key, frame_seq) with TTL aligned to session window. On replay of same frame, drop duplicate credits.
4) Reconciliation job: ingest stream of frame events, group by request idempotency_key, and compute canonical totals. Any runtime that reports per-frame counts must converge to the same canonical total.
5) Back-pressure/resume semantics: when a resume occurs, transcoder must send resume-anchor metadata indicating last accepted frame_seq. Serving runtime will accept only subsequent frames for crediting.

Risks & tradeoffs:
- Slight additional latency from attaching/validating frame metadata (expected < 1ms typical, measurable under load).
- Storage overhead from dedupe state and frame logs; mitigated by short TTL and optional sampling for long-tail debugging.
- Requires changes in some proxies and mobile SDKs for idempotency header support; rollout must include backward compatibility where proxies omit metadata (fall back to conservative crediting with reconciliation tagging).

Open questions:
- Should canonical tokenization happen before or after any model-specific normalization (e.g., prompt templating)? Recommendation: after normalization but before model ingestion; this ensures prompt templates are counted consistently.
- How to handle attachments (binary blobs) where token estimation is nontrivial? Proposal: attachments are pre-hashed and size-based token estimates are attached; we will add a separate ticket to validate attachment-token heuristics.

comments: 2026-03-04 Aisha Patel: Created ticket after SOC team escalated two customer cases with ~+12% charges during websocket resume scenarios.
2026-03-06 Marco Hernandez: Spike complete. Found that some edge proxies rewrite websocket frames which drop our derived frame_seq header causing duplicates.
2026-03-08 Engineering review: Agreed on canonical tokenizer in runtime. Decided to use idempotency_key derived from request UUID + client-nonce.
2026-03-12 SRE: Synthetic replay harness results attached to drive; variance reduced from 3.8% -> 0.05% on prototype under 5k req/s load.
2026-03-14 Marco Hernandez: Updated acceptance criteria to include dashboard reconciliation job. Assigned next steps to SRE and SDK leads for idempotency header support.
